promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

learningObjectives.title: Formation of the Moon (giant impact hypothesis)
The far side of the Moon

questions.q: Which hypothesis is currently the most widely accepted explanation for the origin of the Moon?
options: The giant impact hypothesis
The capture hypothesis
The fission hypothesis
The co-formation (accretion) hypothesis
questions.explain: The giant impact hypothesis, in which a large body struck the early Earth, is the leading model for the Moon's formation.

questions.q: According to the giant impact hypothesis, roughly how large was the body that collided with the early Earth?
options: About the size of Mars
About the size of Jupiter
About the size of a small asteroid
About the size of the present-day Moon
questions.explain: The impactor is thought to have been a Mars-sized planetary body that struck the young Earth.

questions.q: Approximately how long ago is the Moon thought to have formed?
options: About 4.5 billion years ago
About 4.5 million years ago
About 13.8 billion years ago
About 500 million years ago
questions.explain: The Moon formed roughly 4.5 billion years ago, shortly after the early Earth itself.

questions.q: Which observation provides strong evidence in support of the giant impact hypothesis?
options: Moon rocks have oxygen isotope ratios very similar to Earth rocks
The Moon is much denser than the Earth
The Moon has a very large iron core
Moon rocks contain large amounts of liquid water
questions.explain: The close match in oxygen isotope ratios suggests the Moon formed largely from Earth material, as the hypothesis predicts.

questions.q: How does the giant impact hypothesis explain why the Moon has only a very small iron core?
options: Most of the iron stayed with Earth's core, so the debris that formed the Moon was iron-poor
The Moon's iron core evaporated into space soon after it formed
The Moon never came into contact with any iron
The impactor was made entirely of ice
questions.explain: The Moon formed mainly from iron-poor outer/mantle material, since dense iron remained concentrated in Earth's core.

questions.q: A student notes that the Moon's mean density (about 3.3 g/cm3) is much lower than Earth's (about 5.5 g/cm3). Which conclusion best fits the giant impact hypothesis?
options: The Moon formed mainly from low-density rocky mantle material rather than dense iron core material
The Moon must be hollow at its centre
The Moon must have formed far from the Sun
The Moon and Earth cannot share a common origin
questions.explain: A low density is consistent with the Moon being made of rocky mantle debris and little dense iron.

questions.q: Which mission first landed humans on the surface of the Moon?
options: Apollo 11
Apollo 13
Luna 9
Apollo 8
questions.explain: Apollo 11 achieved the first crewed landing on the Moon in 1969.

questions.q: In which year did the first crewed Moon landing take place?
questions.explain: Apollo 11 landed on the Moon in July 1969.

questions.q: Who was the first person to walk on the Moon?
options: Neil Armstrong
Buzz Aldrin
Michael Collins
Yuri Gagarin
questions.explain: Neil Armstrong was the first human to step onto the lunar surface, followed by Buzz Aldrin.

questions.q: The Soviet Union's series of uncrewed spacecraft sent to explore the Moon was known as the:
options: Luna programme
Apollo programme
Gemini programme
Mercury programme
questions.explain: The Soviet Luna programme comprised uncrewed probes, several of which reached and imaged the Moon.

questions.q: Why did Apollo astronauts leave retroreflectors (mirror arrays) on the Moon's surface?
options: To reflect laser beams from Earth so the Earth-Moon distance can be measured precisely
To provide light for future astronauts landing at night
To reflect sunlight and warm the lunar surface
To act as radio aerials for communication with Earth
questions.explain: Lasers fired from Earth reflect off these mirrors, allowing the Earth-Moon distance to be measured very accurately.

questions.q: Why are the lunar rock samples returned by the Apollo missions scientifically valuable?
options: They allow the Moon's composition and age to be studied and formation theories to be tested
They prove the Moon is made mostly of iron
They can be used as fuel for future spacecraft
They show the Moon has a thick atmosphere
questions.explain: Analysing returned samples reveals the Moon's composition and age, helping to test ideas such as the giant impact hypothesis.

questions.q: A space agency is deciding whether to send a robotic probe or a crewed mission to the Moon. Which is a genuine advantage of using a robotic probe?
options: It costs less and puts no human lives at risk
It can always collect and interpret samples better than astronauts
It never needs any communication with Earth
It removes the need for any rocket launch
questions.explain: Robotic probes are cheaper and avoid the danger and life-support demands of sending humans.

questions.q: Which spacecraft first returned photographs of the far side of the Moon?
options: Luna 3
Apollo 11
Sputnik 1
Voyager 1
questions.explain: The Soviet probe Luna 3 sent back the first images of the Moon's far side in 1959.

questions.q: Why do we always see the same face of the Moon from Earth?
options: The Moon's rotation period equals its orbital period around Earth
The Moon does not rotate on its axis at all
The far side is permanently in darkness
The Earth's rotation keeps the same side facing us
questions.explain: Because the Moon spins once for each orbit of Earth (synchronous rotation), the same hemisphere always faces us.

questions.q: What is the name for the situation in which the Moon turns once on its axis in exactly the time it takes to orbit the Earth once?
options: Synchronous rotation
Retrograde rotation
Precession
Refraction
questions.explain: This matching of rotation and orbital period is called synchronous rotation (tidal locking).

questions.q: Why is calling the far side the 'dark side of the Moon' misleading?
options: The far side receives just as much sunlight as the near side over a lunar cycle
The far side is always brighter than the near side
The far side can never be seen by any spacecraft
The far side is permanently frozen and lit by starlight only
questions.explain: Both hemispheres are lit by the Sun in turn as the Moon orbits, so the far side is not permanently dark.

questions.q: How does the far side of the Moon differ in appearance from the near side?
options: It has many more craters and far fewer large dark maria
It is completely smooth with no craters
It is covered by large oceans of liquid water
It has a dense atmosphere hiding its surface
questions.explain: The far side is heavily cratered and has very few of the dark volcanic plains (maria) common on the near side.

questions.q: The Moon's orbital period around the Earth is about 27.3 days. Using the idea of synchronous rotation, roughly how long does the Moon take to spin once on its axis?
options: About 27.3 days
About 24 hours
About 12 hours
About 365 days
questions.explain: Under synchronous rotation the Moon's spin period equals its orbital period, so it is also about 27.3 days.

questions.q: An astronaut is standing near the centre of the far side of the Moon. What would they observe about the Earth?
options: The Earth would never be visible in their sky
The Earth would always be directly overhead
The Earth would rise and set once every day
The Earth would be visible only during a lunar eclipse
questions.explain: Because the same hemisphere always faces Earth, the Earth is never seen from the middle of the far side.
